## Overview & Contribution

Why do infrastructure cost overruns exhibit persistent right-skewness and systematic mean–median gaps? This paper develops a two-level stochastic framework separating **within-project compounding** from **cross-project dependence**:

1. **Within-project multiplicative baseline:** When project costs evolve through sequential proportional updates between baseline and completion, the cost ratio $R = C_a / C_e$ converges under weak dependence toward a **lognormal benchmark**. Compounding alone generates a structural gap between mean and median cost ratios ($\mathbb{E}[R] = \exp(\mu + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2) > \exp(\mu) = \mathrm{Med}[R]$), even when individual stage updates have zero log-drift.
2. **Portfolio aggregation & correlation (Proposition 1):** Under cross-project independence, portfolio aggregation restores asymptotic symmetry by the Central Limit Theorem. Persistent right-skewness at the portfolio level is therefore a mathematical diagnostic of **correlated shocks** (shared macro, regulatory, or factor exposures across projects in a portfolio).
3. **Empirical calibration:** The framework is illustrated across international transport infrastructure datasets (Flyvbjerg), Swedish stage-split transport projects (Eliasson: early plan-to-start stage vs. late start-to-completion stage), and IT project portfolios (Flyvbjerg & Budzier, $N = 4,677$).

> **Key takeaway:** Part of what is commonly attributed purely to behavioral "optimism bias" reflects the structural mathematics of multiplicative compounding combined with correlated portfolio shocks.
